title: A Conversation with James V. Shuls: Restoring the Purpose of American Education
author: Jenna A. Robinson
summary: In this interview, Jenna Robinson speaks with James Shuls of Florida State University's Institute for Governance and Civics about The Phoenix Principles, the book he co-wrote with Jason Bedrick. Shuls argues that American schools have lost sight of their purpose, which he defines as the formation of a person with character, rooted in tradition and history, rather than mere skills or workforce preparation. He explains how truth, goodness and character formation can be pursued even in public schools through deliberate choices about books and exemplars, recalling a teacher who told him the best book his son would read was whatever he liked. He defends the primacy of parents as a pre-political right and criticises the idea that using public benefits requires parents to give up their convictions. He says the most practical implications are for school leaders and board members, who should let the principles drive curriculum, hiring and culture, and he points to Florida as the state closest to adopting them.
points: Shuls defines education as the formation of a person, which shifts the debate from better schooling to a better understanding of schooling's purpose.
Schools committed to truth and character are intentional about curriculum, putting heroes of virtue and moral exemplars in front of children rather than leaving reading to student preference.
The primacy of parents is framed as a primary and pre-political right, so the state should help parents fulfil it instead of requiring them to surrender their convictions.
The book offers principles rather than a policy toolkit, and its practical audience is school leaders and board members who set direction.
Florida's board of education adoption of the principles is offered as the nearest real example of a state following them.
quotes: Education is the formation of a person. We want students formed with character, rooted in our traditions and our history, and with a right-ordered faith in the principles that our nation was built upon.
Today, we seem to have lost this understanding. Education is seen as the activities that take place in school—reading, writing, and arithmetic—or as a means of preparing students for the workforce.
The fact that we even question the role of truth, goodness, and character formation in public schools is an indictment of our modern concept of public education.
When my son entered first grade, I asked his teachers a simple question: “What’s the best book my child will read this year?” The response was appalling: “Whatever he likes.
Rather than demanding submission, the state should help parents exercise their responsibility to educate their children.
School leaders and board members, whether in public or private institutions, can set the direction of a school.

These principles should drive curricular decisions, hiring practices, school culture, routines, and norms. With these principles guiding their decisions, school leaders can be proactive rather than reactive.
Look to Florida. While not perfect, it has come closest to following this path.
